edits.old: HCP Terraform workspaces differ from CLI workspaces: they contain configuration, variables, and state and can have individual access controls. HashiCorp recommends one HCP workspace per infrastructure component per environment. (high confidence)
edits.new: HCP Terraform workspaces differ from CLI workspaces: each contains its own configuration, variables and state, and permissions can be granted to individual users and teams per workspace. HashiCorp recommends splitting large monolithic configurations into smaller ones, each in its own workspace (for example networking-prod, app1-prod, monitoring-prod), which also makes it easy to reuse configurations for other environments. Sources: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/workspaces

evidence.quote: HCP Terraform performs Terraform runs on its own disposable virtual machines, using that workspace's configuration, variables, and state.
You can grant individual users and user groups permissions for one or more workspaces that dictate whether they can manage variables, perform runs, etc.

We recommend that organizations break down large monolithic Terraform configurations into smaller ones, then assign each one to its own workspace and delegate permissions and responsibilities for them.
After splitting the code, you would create "networking-prod", "app1-prod", "monitoring-prod" workspaces, and assign separate teams to manage them.

edits.old: MongoDB recommends separate Atlas projects for application/environment pairs, particularly in production, because project-level settings and permissions define important isolation boundaries. Applying that guidance to Terraform suggests mapping separately controlled deployments to the relevant Atlas projects; directory names or CLI workspace names alone do not enforce those Atlas boundaries. The mapping is an architectural inference, not a MongoDB-mandated repository layout. (medium confidence)
edits.new: MongoDB recommends separate Atlas projects for each application and environment pair, particularly in production, because project-level configurations such as network and security settings define isolation and least-privilege boundaries. Mapping separately controlled Terraform deployments to the relevant Atlas projects is an architectural inference, not a MongoDB-mandated repository layout. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/hierarchy.md
